_source.displaydescription:
Bhulukā (Bhulukhā) Degaḥ, locally known as Santāneśvara Mahādeva, is located at the Yatkhā Ṭola, Naradevi. Since Pruscha (1975, 42) named it as Bhulukā Degaḥ, it is probable that the temple became popular as Santāneśvara Mahādeva only after 1975 CE.

This is a three-storied tiered temple with jhĩgaṭī tiled roofs. The wooden elements used in the temple exhibit a sophisticated craftmanship. Its sanctum can be reached after climbing a flight of stairs since it is elevated on a two-level plinth. The ground floor has a portico supported by twelve wooden pillars (a set of four pillars in each cardinal direction). Pruscha (ibid.) recorded fifty-two struts on which various images of Śiva, Śakti, griffins, and alike have been carved. A Śivaliṅga, wrapped in a silver sheet, is consecrated inside the sanctum. There are statues of numerous deities established inside the wall niches of the sanctum. During its renovation in 2001 CE (VS 2058), all of the existing wooden elements of the temple, except for the rotten and degraded ones, were used. Thus, the temple retains its authenticity.

There are no evidence to appoint the initial construction of the temple. However, local residents believe that Lamba Karṇa Bhaṭṭa, the dīkṣā guru of King Pratāpa Malla (1639 – 1674 CE) built the temple.

A huge aniconic stone can be seen on the northern side of the temple. Locals worship it as Bhairava. It is said that Bhairava including the Eight Mother Godesses (aṣṭamātṛkā) was invoked in many places when the city of Kathmandu was founded. This aniconic stone is one of them and also referred to as a protector (dikpāla). According to a local resident (one of the descendants of Lamba Karṇa Bhaṭṭa, Śarmā, male, age 50) the head of Bhairava is buried underneath the ground since devotees should not look at his ferocious face directly.

In the past, the aforementioned Bhaṭṭa family was responsible for the daily rituals and maintenance of the temple. However, an Upādhyāya caste priest performs the daily ritual in the present-day. A huge bonfire is lit in front of the temple on the day of the Śivarātrī. Mondays of the month of Śrāvana witness a multitude of devotes in the temple. Usually, childless couples perform a special ritual, wishing for offspring.

Tana Bāhā located in Caṃki Ṭola, is a branch of Oku Bāhāḥ (LAL2260). It has no proper shrine to house its principal deity (kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ) Akṣobhya Buddha. Therefore, the deity is kept inside a simple cement plastered structure (locally called kvāḥpādegaḥ) which is capped by a caitya. A dharmadhātujinālaya caitya is established in the courtyard.  No documented evidence is so far traced out to date the Bahā’s initial construction. A narration is circulated amongst the local residents that it was built by certain Śreṣṭhas (Cipālu). The Bāhāḥ got destroyed due course of time and turned into ruins, which was then converted into a female toilet. Once upon a time, a person called Vidyālala Tāmrākāra experienced with his extraordinary sniffing capacity that something important and archeologically valuable is buried underneath the toilet (cf. H. Śākya 1994, 124). The Bāhāḥ’s remnants were found after the site was excavated and it was then rebuilt by Harṣa Bahādura Śākya, a resident of Oṃ Bāhāḥ in NS 1069 (1948 CE). After it was restored, he provided this place for the nuns who practise Sthavīravāda (vernac. Therāvāda) Buddhism. It is called Jayamaṅgala Vihāra since then. The Bāhāḥ is still inhabited by such nuns and the decedents of Harṣa Bahādura Śākya have been performing the daily rituals here.[1]

Footnotes

  1. ^ Although the ritual is called daily ‘nitya’ thus needs to be performed every day, they perform it only after certain intervals.

_source.displaydescription:
Kvātha Bāhāḥ is a branch of Oku Bāhāḥ (LAL2260). It is located on the way to Thainā Ṭola from Saugah. The Bāhāḥ’s shrine for the principal deity (dyaḥchẽ) is not in front of its main east-facing gate but faces north. Unlike other Bāhāḥs, its premises are not in a square shape but in an elongated rectangular shape that stretches from north to south. This was not always the case. 

The Bāhāḥ’s old structure can be seen in the historical photos published by Pruscha (1975,199). It shows intricately designed timber posts on the ground floor of the dyaḥchẽ and equally beautiful trikhājhyāḥ on the first. The statue of the esoteric deity (āgãdyaḥ), which used to be located on the first floor, is now stolen. At present, the Bāhāḥ’s dyaḥchẽ has been completely privatized and is replaced by a residential house. Similarly, the phalcā on the right and left side of the main Bāhāḥ entrance is merged into the private house.

It is difficult to ascertain which deity was housed as the Bāhā’s principal deity (kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ) because of the theft of the kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ’s icon. However, the members of the saṅgha mention that the icon of Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara, made with sandalwood, was consecrated as the kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ. Based on this belief, a stone icon of Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara is placed where the old dyaḥchẽ used to be. The icon of Triratnas is placed on top of Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara’s statue. Locke (1985, 112), however, mentions that it is Akṣobhya, and not Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara, established as the kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ, and that kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ’s icon was mistakenly positioned in the east.
 
There is no inscriptive evidence about the Bāhāḥ’s construction date and its benefactor. The Sanskrit name of this Bāhāḥ is Kuṭusiṃha Vihāra. Another Bāhāḥ, Jothā Bāhāḥ, is adjacent to the Kvātha Bāhāḥ. The local residents believe that Kuṭusiṃha made this Bāhāḥ after his brother, Jōdhāju, constructed the Jothā Bāhāḥ. There is no independent saṅgha of the Bāhāḥ.
 
Both Jothā Bāhāḥ and Kvātha Bāhāḥ are members of one saṅgha. A single temple caretaker (dyaḥpāḥlāḥ) performs the daily worship for both the Bāhāḥs. A Śākya family in Patan, members of this saṅgha, goes by the name of Narsingh Khalaḥ. Anniversary worship (varṣavardhana) of both of these Bāhāḥs used to happen on the same day. With the extinction of the Bāhāḥ’s dyaḥchẽ, the anniversary worship has also vanished.  
 
There is a Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya built in NS 980 (1860 CE) on the Bāhāḥ’s premises.

As it the case of most of the Gaṇeśa Mandiras in the Kathmandu Valley, this Mandira, too, faces, south. The local residents of Tyāgala Ṭola worship this Gaṇeśa as their area deity (sthāna). It is built in a pagoda-style and has three storeys. The main door to the sanctum is flanked by a pair of lions, and an artistically carved toraṇa with the images of Gaṇeśa (in the centre) and two people playing the musical instrument mṛdaṅga (in the left and right) is kept above the door.  The images of Śiva, Gaṇeśa, and Mātṛkā Goddesses have been carved on the struts supporting the roofs. The last roof of the temple is metal tiled, however, the first and second roofs are tiled with jhĩgaṭī bricks. The photograph published by Pruscha (1975, p. 189) shows an additional pinnacle erected on the roof of the second floor. However, this pinnacle is not there anymore.

No documented evidence is so far traced out which records the date of the temple’s initial construction. The date inscribed on the toraṇa in Nepāla Calendar Era could be the date of the initial construction. However, since the middle numeral of this date is defaced, its exact dating remains obscure. Pruscha (1975, p. 189) has mentioned that a guṭhī was established in NS 768 (1648 CE) to sponsor the daily and occasion rituals for this temple. He also informs us that the struts supporting the roofs were carved in NS 863 (1743 CE). Since he does not validate this information through any documented evidence, its authenticity remains questionable.

An inscription from NS 853 (1733 CE) is kept inside the sanctum. It records about the establishment of a guṭhī that is responsible to sponsor the rituals for the caitya erected in front of this Gaṇeśa Mandira. The Mandira was renovated in VS 2060 (2003 CE) by the Department of Archelogy (source: Local knowledge, a resident of the area, Maharjana, male, age 49). The specific iconographical features of the Gaṇeśa statue[1] of this temple suggest that it is one of the oldest Gaṇeśas from the Kathmandu Valley dating back from the 5th to 7th century.

There are three separate guṭhīs of Jyāpus, Mulmīs, and Bārāhīs of Tyāgala Ṭola related to this temple. The Jyāpus’ guṭhī sponsors ritual worship to Gaṇeśa on the day called Picāśa Caturdaśī followed by an animal sacrifice. The Mulmīs’ guṭhī worship Gaṇeśa on the day of Indrajātrā procession and Piśāca Caturdaśī and displays a metal Gaṇeśa statue in the temple for the public, which is also followed by an animal sacrifice. The Bārāhī’s gūṭhī too organises special worship for Gaṇeśa every year, on the day of Kuśe Aũśī followed by the sacrifice of a he-goat. In addition to these guṭhīs, a separate guṭhī of the Jyāpus of Tyāgala Ṭola too places a toraṇa above the main statue in the sanctum and displays it publicly twice a year.

Footnotes

  1. ^ For example, it has two arms, a big belly, is not adorned with pieces of jewellery, is in the ardhaparyaṅka position, its trunk is slightly twisted to the right and it is not accompanied by other statues, such as his family members and transporter (see Khanāla VS 2074, 163 for the iconographical features of the old Gaṇeśa statues in the Kathmandu Valley).

Jena Bāhāḥ, also known as Śrī Jñāna Nāma Vihāra, is located on the southern side of Jena Bāhāḥ Ṭola in front of the Gaṇeśa Mandira (LAL0270). The courtyard can be accessed by passing through a metal door. The main structure of the bāhāḥ has mostly collapsed. Its foundations as well as wooden decorative elements are scattered around the site. The main structure on the left side of the metal door has been destroyed and is fenced off with CGI sheets. The square courtyard has a teliya tiled floor and contains a Licchavi caitya, a dharmadhātu maṇḍala at the southeastern corner and a Kṛṣṇa shrine with a brick dome at the center. To the south, one can also find a Durgā shrine raised on a platform 90 cm in height.

This bāhāḥ is a branch of Hakha Bāhāḥ (LAL0390). The building lacks a dyaḥchẽ, something which is normally a major feature of such bāhāḥ. Local people say that it was probably destroyed during the 1934 earthquake and never reconstructed. Locke (1985, 152) assumes that the bāhāḥ was abandoned after the earthquake. Later, Pradhānas, non-Buddhist Newar families from Kathmandu, bought the surrounding lands and constructed houses upon it. These buildings now surround the bāhāḥ area. There is no inscription at the site through which one could date the monument. Locke (1985, 154) argues that this branch predates the transfer of Hakha Bāhāḥ from its original place to its present location. This move took place during the reign of Siddhi Narasiṃha Malla (1620-1661). The Licchavi caitya in the bāhāḥ's courtyard supports this hypothesis.

Guitaḥ Gaṇeśa Mandira (Temple) is located behind the waterspout at the Guitaḥ Ṭola, and faces west. Generally, each Newar city quarter (ṭola) in the Kathmandu Valley has one Gaṇeśa temple, but there are two at the Guitaḥ Ṭola. The Guitaḥ Gaṇeśa Temple was constructed from the Guṭhī comprising Śākyas and Maharjana caste members of the Ṭola. This one-storey Temple stands on a relatively tall plinth and is tiled with jhĩgaṭīs. The roof is capped by a metal pinnacle which is flanked by a pair of metal flags. A long metal banner (patāḥ) connected to the base of the pinnacle is hanging down up to the eves board.

The door to the sanctum is capped by a carved wooden toraṇa and is flanked by a pair of lions. A dancing Gaṇeśa image is carved on the middle of the toraṇa and a Buddha image is carved on either side of Gaṇeśa. The sanctum of the Temple houses a stone statue of Gaṇeśa whose head is capped by a metal crown (mukuṭa). L. Bangdel (1995, 230) has dated this statue to the 18th century CE. There are some other statues established on the plinth of the Temple. Among them, the Śiva statue (LAL2030-010), which Bangdel (1995, 229) has identified as Viṣṇu, is said to be from the 14th century CE. The statue of Viṣṇu (LAL2030-012) is dated to 15th Century CE, and the statue of Umāmaheśvara (LAL2030-009) is said to be from the 17th century CE (cf. Bangdel L. 1995, 229). Moreover, there is also a Sarasvatī statue (LAL2030-011) established in 1775 CE (NS 895) by a certain monk īndrajyoti.

We have no historical sources to date the initial construction of the Temple. In 2008 CE (VS 2065), it was reconstructed with the financial support from the Lalitpur Municipality.

The above mentioned Guṭhī currently (as of June 2021) has nine members (two Śākyas and seven Maharjanas). On the day of the Gũlā Pāru (the first day of the bright fortnight of Bhādra), the Guṭhī members place a brass Gaṇeśa statue in front of the main statue inside the sanctum for public display and worship it. A similar ritual is conducted also on the day of the Indra Jātrā Festival. On this day, samaybaji is offered to the deity.
_source.displayname: Guitaḥ Gaṇeśa Mandira || गुइत: गणेश मन्दिर ।। LAL2030

The sanctum of the Temple houses a stone statue of Gaṇeśa whose head is capped by a metal crown (mukuṭa). L. Bangdel (1995, 230) has dated this statue to the 18th century CE. There are some other statues established on the plinth of the Temple. Among them, the Śiva statue (LAL2030-010), which Bangdel (1995, 229) has identified as Viṣṇu, is said to be from the 14th century CE. The statue of Viṣṇu (LAL2030-012) is dated to 15th Century CE, and the statue of Umāmaheśvara (LAL2030-009) is said to be from the 17th century CE (cf. Bangdel L. 1995, 229). Moreover, there is also a Sarasvatī statue (LAL2030-011) established in 1775 CE (NS 895) by a certain monk īndrajyoti.

We have no historical sources to date the initial construction of the Temple. In 2008 CE (VS 2065), it was reconstructed with the financial support from the Lalitpur Municipality.

The above mentioned Guṭhī currently (as of June 2021) has nine members (two Śākyas and seven Maharjanas). On the day of the Gũlā Pāru (the first day of the bright fortnight of Bhādra), the Guṭhī members place a brass Gaṇeśa statue in front of the main statue inside the sanctum for public display and worship it. A similar ritual is conducted also on the day of the Indra Jātrā Festival. On this day, samaybaji is offered to the deity.

This group of three objects is located to the west of Karuṇāmaya Mandira (BUN0001). The brick pedestal supports a massive stone slab (131cm x 62 cm), upon which the Licchavi Caitya, the Buddha statue and the dome fragment have been loosely placed. This Caitya was constructed some time in the Licchavi period and stands testament to the antiquity of the Bungamati settlement.

The Licchavi Caitya is eroded, slightly damaged and missing its finial. Parts of the right hand and leg of the Buddha statue have broken off, most of the nimbus is missing and the damaged head has been patched up with cement mortar. The dome fragment is missing its finial and its lower part sits to the right of the statue.

This collection of items was obviously quite recently assembled, and it is not known where the large stone base came from. Locals worship the Caitya during their morning visit to the temples. Besides that, other regular worships are not observed at this Caitya.

Pānda Bāhāḥ is located at Ghavāḥ Nani in Lukhusi Ṭola. Unlike most of the bāhāḥs in Patan, this one belongs to the Maharjanas, and not to the Vajrācāryas or Śākyas. Therefore, it has neither a shrine (kvāḥpāḥchẽ) for the Bāhāḥ’s primary deity (kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ), nor a saṅgha.

A small shrine is built in the south-western corner of the Ghavāḥ Nani. The bell-shaped shrine is painted in white, capped by a caitya-shaped pinnacle, and encircled by the serpents (nāga). A stone statue of Akṣobhya flanked by Prajñāpāramitā and Lokeśvara is enshrined inside the shrine’s sanctum sanctorum as kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ. A Pañcāvalīyukta Caitya, Gaṇeśa, and Mahākāla statue are installed in the Bāhāḥ premises.

Pānda Bāhāḥ was built in NS 997 (1877 CE) by Kiṣṇa (text: Kṛṣṇa) Maharjana and his wife Tuyu (Lakṣmīdevī) living in Lukhusi Ṭola. They also established the Pañcāvalīyukta Caitya in the Bāhāḥ premises and formed a guṭhī to worship it in NS 1000 (1880 CE). The decedents of the Bāhāḥ’s founders (especially three families) are still performing the daily rituals. The anniversary celebration of the Bāhāḥ takes places every year, on the full moon day of Āśvina.
